I.     INTRODUCTION

       On one thing SPP and Entergy can agree—the “backdrop” or context against which

a cost allocation methodology is developed matters.8 Under the traditional generator

interconnection and affected system study processes, a generation interconnection request

is studied to determine whether it “breaks” the system—i.e., does it push an existing

constrained facility beyond a pre-defined limit. If so, the costs of any network upgrades

       B.      Entergy Answer Misconstrues Cost Allocation Precedent

       Relying on Coalition of MISO Transmission Customers v. FERC, Entergy argues

that the court has explicitly recognized the right of a customer to challenge the application

of an ex ante cost allocation rule on an as-applied basis.39 But, while Coalition surmised

that an as-applied challenge to a cost allocation method could be pursued, this was dicta

that did not elaborate on how such a challenge could be brought. The court only noted that

a challenge could occur “before the horse has left the barn”—i.e., before a project is

assigned to a transmission owner to construct.40 That is certainly not the case here. The

horse has in fact left the barn—the JTIQ Upgrades are already being constructed by various

transmission owners under a cost allocation framework that was approved by the

Commission and that Entergy did not challenge before the upgrades at issue were in

progress. This is a starkly different posture than what the court speculated in Coalition

may be appropriate; Entergy’s so-called “as-applied” challenge simply comes too late.
